scenarios.title: The date arrives before the estimate
scenarios.prompt: A sponsor says the migration should finish in twelve weeks. The delivery team then estimates each work package while that date remains visible.
scenarios.question: What should the team do before negotiating the final schedule?

options.text: Build an independent range from work packages and assumptions before comparing it with the twelve-week target.
Split twelve weeks across the work packages so every activity fits the target.
Ask the sponsor to repeat why twelve weeks is important and use that as the baseline.

scenarios.explanation: The target can become the reference point for every later estimate. An independent estimate preserves a separate baseline and makes any movement toward the target inspectable.
missingEvidence: Independent estimates from the delivery team.
scenarios.evidenceNote: The visible target creates an anchoring risk, but the final schedule may still converge on twelve weeks if independent evidence supports it.
scenarios.nextAction: Produce a range without the target in view and record why it changes after comparison.

scenarios.title: A detailed plan with no outside view
scenarios.prompt: A team has a detailed task plan for a data migration. It predicts 40 days, but nobody has checked how long similar migrations actually took.
scenarios.question: Which evidence should be added first?

options.text: More detail inside the current plan until every day is allocated.
A reference class of comparable completed migrations and their actual duration range.
A vote on whether 40 days feels optimistic or pessimistic.

scenarios.explanation: More inside detail can improve execution planning without correcting the baseline. Reference-class forecasting tests the plan against completed cases.
missingEvidence: Reasons this project differs from the reference class.
The distribution, not only the best or worst example.
scenarios.evidenceNote: Planning fallacy is a plausible lens when the estimate relies mainly on the inside plan. A poor reference class can also mislead, so comparability must be explained.
scenarios.nextAction: Set an outside-view range first, then document any evidence-based adjustment.

scenarios.title: One failed project resets every estimate
scenarios.prompt: The previous project missed its date by six months. Managers now double every estimate, even though most comparable projects had much smaller delays.
scenarios.question: What is the best way to use the recent failure?

options.text: Ignore it because unusual failures contain no useful information.
Treat it as one observation inside a broader reference class and identify whether the same failure conditions apply.
Use it as the default scenario because recent events are the safest guide.

scenarios.explanation: The vivid failure deserves inspection, but not automatic dominance. A reference class shows how common that outcome is and whether the same conditions are present.
missingEvidence: Frequency of similar delays in comparable work.
Specific causes of the previous failure.
Whether those causes exist in the new project.
scenarios.evidenceNote: Availability bias may explain why the recent failure receives extra weight. The failure can still justify a larger estimate when relevant conditions repeat.
scenarios.nextAction: Add the failed project to the reference class and state the conditions that warrant moving toward its outcome.
